findings.lesson_title: The Five Pillars, the Ten Obligatory Acts and Worship
findings.claim: Salah verse: "Maintain with care the [obligatory] prayers and [in particular] the middle prayer and stand before Allah, devoutly obedient" (Surah 4:103, an-Nisa)
findings.issue: Wrong Surah reference. The verse about guarding prayers and especially 'the middle prayer' is Surah 2:238 (al-Baqarah), not 4:103. Surah 4:103 states that prayer is decreed at specified times but says nothing about the middle prayer.
findings.source: Quran.com Sahih International — 2:238: 'Maintain with care the [obligatory] prayers and [in particular] the middle prayer and stand before Allah, devoutly obedient.'; 4:103 does not contain this wording.

findings.lesson_title: The Five Pillars, the Ten Obligatory Acts and Worship
findings.claim: Jummah prayer verse: "O you who have believed, when [the adhan] is called for the prayer on the day of Jumu'ah [Friday], then proceed to the remembrance of Allah" (Surah 62:10, al-Jumuah)
findings.issue: Wrong verse number. This text is Surah 62:9, not 62:10. Surah 62:10 is the subsequent verse about dispersing after prayer is completed.
findings.source: Quran.com Sahih International — 62:9 contains the adhan/Jumu'ah text; 62:10 is about dispersing after prayer ends.

findings.claim: Mika'il is described as 'the guardian of paradise and bringer of thunder and rain'
findings.issue: Mika'il's role as bringer of rain/provision/sustenance is accurate, but 'guardian of paradise' is incorrect. The guardian/gatekeeper of paradise in Islamic tradition is Ridwan (Malik al-Jannah), not Mika'il. Attributing this role to Mika'il is a factual error.
findings.correction: Remove 'guardian of paradise' from Mika'il's description. Mika'il is associated with rain, provision and sustenance. The guardian of paradise is Ridwan — if needed, add Ridwan as a separate named angel.
findings.source: Islamic tradition: Ridwan is identified in Hadith literature (Sahih Muslim) and tafsir as the guardian of paradise. Mika'il's role relates to rain and provision (rizq). No authoritative source assigns paradise guardianship to Mika'il.

findings.claim: A well-known hadith 'attributed to the Prophet Muhammad after a military campaign, describes him as saying they had returned from the lesser struggle to the greater struggle — the struggle against the self'
findings.issue: This hadith (al-jihad al-akbar vs al-jihad al-asghar) is considered weak (da'if) or fabricated (mawdu') by the majority of major hadith scholars, including Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, Ibn Taymiyyah, and al-Albani. It does not appear in any of the six canonical Sahih collections. The lesson presents it without caveat, which may mislead students about its reliability.
findings.correction: Add a caveat: describe it as 'a widely-cited saying attributed to the Prophet, though its chain of transmission is disputed by many hadith scholars.' The theological concept it expresses remains widely taught across Islamic traditions.
findings.source: Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani (Takhreej Ahadith al-Ihya), al-Albani (Silsilah al-Da'ifah), Ibn Taymiyyah — all classify this hadith as unreliable. Not in Bukhari, Muslim, or the other four canonical collections.

findings.claim: Surah 74:38 quoted as: "Every soul, for what it has earned, will be detained"
findings.issue: The verse reference (al-Muddathir 74:38) is correct, but the translation is a loose paraphrase. Dominant translations (Sahih International, Pickthall, Yusuf Ali) render the Arabic as 'held in pledge for what it has earned' or 'pledged for what it earned' — not 'detained' or 'held responsible.' The lesson presents this as a direct quotation.
findings.correction: Change to 'held in pledge for what it has earned' (Sahih International) or remove the quotation marks to indicate it is a paraphrase.
findings.source: Quran.com Sahih International 74:38: 'Every soul, for what it has earned, will be retained [i.e., held in pledge].'
